title: A sudden change in confusion
summary: Sudden confusion is not 'just the dementia'. Get help today.
callNow: Signs of a stroke: one side of the face droops, one arm is weak, speech is slurred or strange
They is hard to wake, or passes out
Fever with shivering, cold or clammy skin, a fast pulse, or very fast or slow breathing
The confusion started after a head injury
They has diabetes and the confusion came on suddenly

steps.title: Notice how fast it changed
steps.text: Dementia changes slowly, over months. A big change over hours or a day or two is different, and often has a cause that can be treated.

steps.title: Keep them safe and calm
steps.text: Stay with them, speak softly, keep the room quiet and lit. Don't argue with what they says.

steps.title: If nothing on the 911 list is true, call the doctor today
steps.text: Call your loved one's doctor's office or after-hours line now, not tomorrow. A nurse can tell you whether to come in, go to urgent care or go to the emergency room.

steps.title: Tell them what changed
steps.text: When it started, what's different from your loved one's usual, and anything new: a new medicine, a fall, a fever, drinking less, trouble passing urine, pain, poor sleep.

steps.title: Bring the list
steps.text: If they goes to be seen, bring all your loved one's medicines (or photos of the labels) and your notes.

then: Confusion like this can come and go during the day. Better moments don't mean it's over: follow up until the cause is found.
Add what happened to the doctor-visit sheet.
dont: Don't wait until morning to see if it passes.
Don't give extra or new medicines to calm them unless a doctor or pharmacist tells you to.

sources.name: NHS, confusion: common causes in older people
